quiz.q: What does `a + b` actually desugar to in Rust?
options: A special compiler intrinsic with no trait involved
Add::add(a, b)
a.plus(b)
std::ops::plus(a, b)
quiz.explain: Every operator in Rust is shorthand for a trait method call. `+` specifically maps to the Add trait's add method.

quiz.q: Which trait must you implement to make `p1 + p2` work for a custom struct Point?
options: std::ops::Add
std::ops::Index
std::cmp::PartialEq
std::fmt::Display
quiz.explain: Add is the trait behind the + operator. It has an associated Output type and an add(self, rhs) -> Output method.

quiz.q: What does implementing Index<(usize, usize)> for a Grid type enable?
options: grid.get(row, col)
grid[(row, col)] subscript syntax
Automatic sorting of grid cells
grid == grid comparisons
quiz.explain: Index (and IndexMut for read-write) is the trait behind [] syntax — implementing it for your own type lets container[key] work.

quiz.q: A type implements Add but a program tries to use `p += other`. What happens?
options: It works automatically since += is just repeated +
It fails to compile — AddAssign is a separate trait from Add and must be implemented separately
It compiles but silently does nothing
It only works if the type is Copy
quiz.explain: += is backed by the AddAssign trait, distinct from Add. Implementing Add does not give you += for free — you must implement AddAssign too.

quiz.q: Why does `impl Add for Point` typically require Point to be Copy (or otherwise handle ownership explicitly)?
options: Because Add requires Copy by definition and won't compile otherwise
Because Add::add takes self by value, which moves (or copies, for Copy types) the left-hand operand
Because Rust requires all operator traits to only work on Copy types
It has nothing to do with ownership at all
quiz.explain: Most std::ops traits consume self by value. For a Copy type, p1 + p2 copies p1 instead of moving it, so p1 remains usable afterward. For non-Copy types you'd need to implement Add for references or accept the move.

quiz.q: When is operator overloading a GOOD idea according to the lesson's judgment call?
options: Whenever it saves a few characters of typing
When the operator's meaning is exactly what a reader would expect from ordinary math or collection syntax
Only for numeric types built into std
Never — named methods are always better
quiz.explain: Point + Point reading as vector addition, or grid[(row, col)] reading as indexing, are cases where the operator's meaning is obvious and unsurprising — that's when overloading helps rather than confuses.

quiz.q: Why is `+` with side effects (like writing to a file) considered a mistake?
options: Because it would cause a compile error
Because readers bring assumptions to + from ordinary math and don't expect side effects or mutation
Because + can only be implemented for numeric types
It isn't a mistake, it's fine practice
quiz.explain: Operators carry implicit expectations. A + that mutates or has side effects violates those expectations — a named method (like log.append(entry)) communicates intent far more clearly.

quiz.q: What does Index::index return, and how does `grid[(1, 2)]` end up as a value instead of a reference?
options: index returns a value directly; no dereferencing happens
index returns a reference (&Output), and the [] syntax automatically dereferences it
index always panics and grid[] never actually calls it
grid[(1,2)] calls .clone() internally on Output
quiz.explain: Index::index returns &Output. The compiler's desugaring of container[key] automatically dereferences that reference, so you see the value directly.

flashcards.front: What does `a + b` desugar to in Rust?
flashcards.back: Add::add(a, b). Every operator is a trait method call under familiar symbolic syntax.

flashcards.front: Which trait/method pair implements the + operator for a custom type?
flashcards.back: std::ops::Add, with an associated type Output and a method fn add(self, rhs: Self) -> Self::Output.
std::ops::Index (read) and std::ops::IndexMut (read-write). index() returns &Output, which [] auto-dereferences.

flashcards.front: Does implementing Add give you += for free?
flashcards.back: No. += is backed by a separate trait, AddAssign, with its own add_assign(&mut self, rhs) method. You must implement it separately.

flashcards.front: Why does Point usually derive Copy when implementing Add?
flashcards.back: Most std::ops traits take self by value, which moves the operand. Deriving Copy means p1 + p2 copies p1 instead of consuming it, so p1 stays usable afterward.

flashcards.front: When should you overload an operator vs use a named method?
flashcards.back: Overload when the meaning is unambiguous and matches what a reader expects from ordinary math/collection syntax (Point + Point, grid[(r,c)]). Use a named method when the operator's meaning would surprise the reader (e.g. a + with side effects).

flashcards.front: Name three operators and their backing std::ops traits.
flashcards.back: + -> Add, - -> Sub, * -> Mul (also += -> AddAssign, -= -> SubAssign, [] -> Index/IndexMut).
